newsitem.title: UK: Funds shave U.S. holdings, emerging mkts in focus.
newsitem.headline: Funds shave U.S. holdings, emerging mkts in focus.

text.p: Fund managers are continuing to reduce their exposure to U.S. equities, but are finding few obvious alternatives in currently uncertain world markets.
They told Reuters that cash and emerging markets were attracting an increasing slice of global liquidity, with many managers prepared to accept a pullback after steep growth in 1996.
A monthly global asset allocation survey of mostly UK-based fund managers showed a reduction in U.S. equity and bond allocations.
But strategists said a lack of obvious alternatives had left some players sticking to benchmarks awaiting further direction.
"Just at the moment I wouldn't go out and buy an awful lot," said Nick Knight, analyst at Nomura Research Institute.
Matthew Merritt, ING Barings analyst, said expected limited interest rate rises in the U.S. would spark near term volatility, and this would be felt outside the U.S.
"If we did hit that volatility then it is not going to be particularly comfortable in all financial markets."
Knight said many managers were not expecting a major reversal.
"There has been a relatively complacent mindset. The more interesting test will come at lower levels I suspect, when we have fallen another couple of hundred points.
"Then you'll see the whites of their eyes. Are they really saying it is just a pullback or will they then start to panic and deliver us another couple of hundred points.
Merritt, recently an advocate of a heavily overweight continental European position, said valuations were being pushed to extremes there and profits should be taken or positions scaled back.
He said the UK would be an obvious play following an expected Labour victory in the general election on May 1.

A clarification of Labour policy following the election, especially on corporate taxation, could be a trigger for a shift into the UK, "to potentially unleash some of the value in the UK which stacks up on simple valuation".

In the US, Merritt said a long bond move through seven percent could take some of the excesses off equity markets, but as long as interest rate rises were not protracted then the investment environment for 1997 remained relatively favourable.
Knight said that U.S. bonds could benefit from a move out of cash, especially if the U.S. long bond moved substantially through seven percent.

"Technically there is not a lot between 7.00 percent and 7.30 so we could be looking at quite a nasty knock on the bonds. When it comes to reinvest am I going buy U.S. bonds at 7.30 or the Dow at 6,600. It is not an easy choice."

Scudder, Stevens and Clark Ltd's portfolio team said it was maintaining an underweight U.S. position, having shown above benchmark returns with that stance in February. In bonds, it said it was moving limited positions into countries such as Poland, Czechoslovakia, Thailand and El Salvador.
"Generally we are staying with markets not correlated to the U.S., especially the global bond fund," a Scudder spokeswoman said.
Knight said emerging markets may offer a relative play on a general pullback in world markets, but were unlikely to attract major flows.
"It is a bit of a leap of faith that the guy selling the UK goes and buys India. He might but more likely he will head for the hills," Knight said.
Merritt said emerging markets are not immune to U.S. market volatility, but the scope for further gains remained quite strong.

Emerging markets had not performed on the upside for much of the past two years and were likely to be a relatively better play than developed markets, with the short term offering the best opportunities following a pullback in the sector in recent weeks.
LGT broker services manager Caroline Carroll said it had slightly increased its exposure to emerging markets, and remained confident about continental Europe.

The majority of the increase in emerging market allocation was to South Africa, which she said was "the one economy in the world that we know for definite will have falling interest rates this year", possibly as much as three percent.
